Why calculators can show different results

Same question, different assumptions

  • Your schedule matters: results use the hours and paid weeks you enter — a 2,080-hour year (40 × 52) is only the default, not your schedule.
  • Gross, not net: these tools show pay before income tax, Social Security, Medicare, and benefit deductions.
  • Rules vary: overtime eligibility, the regular rate, and state rules are not decided by the calculator — they come from your pay arrangement.
  • Averages, not checks: monthly and semi-monthly figures are annual averages (annual ÷ 12 or ÷ 24), not four weekly checks added together.

Worked example

$20 an hour, 40 regular hours + 10 extra hours, time and a half (1.5×).

StepMathResult
1. Overtime rate$20 × 1.5$30 an hour
2. Regular and overtime pay$20 × 40 = $800; $30 × 10 = $300$800 + $300
3. Total weekly pay$800 + $300$1,100 a week

Total: $1,100 a week ($300 from overtime).

Note: Gross pay, before tax. Overtime eligibility and the regular rate depend on your pay arrangement — this is the standard 1.5× model, not a legal determination.

What this calculator does not do

  • Gross pay only — before tax and deductions.
  • Overtime eligibility and the regular rate depend on your pay arrangement; the calculator does not decide them.
  • Daily thresholds follow the CA-style model only when you select the daily rule.

How is overtime pay calculated?

Overtime rate & earnings

Regular rate × multiplier = overtime rate
Overtime rate × extra hours = overtime pay

$25 × 1.5 × 10 = $375

Total gross earnings

Regular rate × regular hours + overtime pay

$25 × 40 + $375 = $1,375

Time and a half vs. double time

Time and a half uses a 1.5× rate. Double time uses a 2× rate. These are calculation scenarios; the tool does not determine which multiplier applies to your job.

For California-style daily rules, switch the overtime rule above to Daily rule: hours over 8 in a day are priced at 1.5×, hours over 12 at 2×, and a 7th consecutive day prices its first 8 hours at 1.5×. Daily overtime hours do not count again toward the weekly 40-hour threshold — weekly overtime is added only on the hours that remain.

Overtime eligibility and rates

Rules can depend on location, worker classification, and the employment arrangement. This tool estimates the arithmetic from your inputs. It does not determine entitlement, exemptions, or a legally required regular rate.

For U.S. employees, see the Department of Labor’s overtime guidance. Check the guidance that applies to your own situation.

The 2026 overtime tax deduction

Separate from how overtime is calculated, U.S. federal tax law now lets many workers deduct the premium half of time-and-a-half pay — the 0.5 part above the regular rate — up to set caps for tax years 2025–2028. Withholding does not change during the year; the benefit arrives when you file. Our guide to the no tax on overtime deduction explains who qualifies, what counts, and how reporting works.

Does this calculate take-home pay?

Wage conversions show earnings before deductions. A bank deposit may be lower after taxes, benefit premiums, retirement contributions, and other payroll deductions. The paycheck calculator can subtract amounts you enter, and also shows a federal-only take-home estimate (2026 brackets + FICA; state tax excluded).

Frequently asked questions

What is overtime pay?

It is pay calculated for hours treated as overtime under an employment arrangement or applicable rules. This tool applies the multiplier to the extra hours you enter.

How do I calculate time and a half?

Multiply the regular hourly rate by 1.5. A $25 rate becomes $37.50 per overtime hour.

How much is $20 an hour with overtime?

At a 1.5× multiplier, the overtime rate is $30 an hour. Regular hours remain at $20.

How much is $25 an hour with overtime?

At 1.5×, extra hours are modeled at $37.50 each. Ten overtime hours produce $375 of overtime pay.

What does double time mean?

It means a rate multiplied by two. A $25 regular rate becomes $50 per double-time hour.

Can I change the overtime multiplier?

Yes. Choose 1.25×, 1.5×, 2×, or Custom, then enter your own multiplier.

Does this handle California-style daily overtime?

Yes. Switch the overtime rule to Daily rule and enter hours per day and days per week. Hours over 8 in a day are priced at 1.5×, hours over 12 at 2×, and a 7th consecutive day prices its first 8 hours at 1.5×. Daily overtime hours are excluded from the weekly 40-hour count, so weekly overtime is added only on the remaining hours.

Does overtime affect annual earnings?

Yes in this model. Weekly overtime pay is multiplied by the paid weeks entered. Actual overtime availability can vary.

Can salaried employees receive overtime?

Eligibility depends on the applicable rules and worker classification. The salary label alone does not answer that question.

Is overtime always due after 40 hours?

This calculator does not determine thresholds or eligibility. Check the rules that apply to the specific role and location.

Does the result include taxes?

No. Regular, overtime, weekly, and annual totals are all gross figures.

Overtime calculator methodology

Visible assumptions. Checkable formulas.

Regular weekly pay is rate × regular hours. Overtime pay is rate × multiplier × extra hours. Annual estimates multiply the weekly total by paid weeks. Daily-rule mode prices each day separately (1.5× after 8 hours, 2× after 12, day-7 rule) and adds weekly overtime only on hours not already paid as daily overtime. Values retain full precision until display. Read our calculation methodology.

References

The official sources behind the 2026 figures used across this site's calculators:

  • IRS Publication 15-T — federal income tax withholding methods.
  • IRS 401(k) contribution limits — the 2026 elective deferral limit (Notice 2025-67).
  • Social Security Administration — contribution and benefit base ($184,500 for 2026).
  • U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division — FLSA overtime pay requirements.
  • Bureau of Labor Statistics, Employer Costs for Employee Compensation — benefits' share of total compensation.
